chapter_theme: The women play on the gem hill, dressing the stones as grass and flowers and singing the king's deeds; the king has a god take the form of a rutting elephant to frighten them, then comforts them, goes down at noon to the pool, and enters it with them, where the swirling water begins a water-fight.

cast.role: Tivittan, the dark gem-hued lord, the king
the god the king commands to become an elephant
the king's attendants at the pool

1651.reading: The women of the court clear the gems that the stream has washed down the misty slope and, laying out streets, build a fine toy city.
1651.nuance: The sense of சீலம் புனைவார் in line 3 is not fixed; read here as the women giving the play-city its fitting adornment.
1651.event: The women build a toy city from the gems the stream brought down.

1652.reading: Women call the emerald's cool rays tender grass, step on them gingerly, and, their small feet aching, sink softly onto a bed of flowers.
1652.event: The women walk on gem-light as on grass, and rest on a flower bed.

1653.reading: Seeing the fresh-leaved grove and saying it is like their lord, the women bathe in the gem waterfall with a fresh glow of love in their looks.
1653.nuance: Line 3 makes the grove's beauty a likeness of the king; the women's love shapes how they see the place.
1653.event: The women praise the grove as like their lord and bathe in the waterfall.

1654.reading: Taking the cool moonstone, bright inside, for the moon, the women see the drops it throws as rain from a cloud and hide in the grove.
1654.nuance: The verse is built on mistaking: stone for moon, drops for rain.
1654.event: The women mistake moonstone drops for cloud rain and hide in the grove.

1655.reading: The women stroke the ruby's red rays with their ring-bright fingers, calling them ashoka sprouts, and bend over them with a small smile.
1655.event: The women take ruby rays for ashoka shoots and stroke them.

1656.reading: Seeing a great shining ruby, the women think of it as kaya flowers fit for the hair; bees follow, and they cover their eyes and walk on.
1656.nuance: Line 2 reads the gem as blossom and line 3 the women as ready to wear it; the last line's covered eyes is read as a play against the following bees.
1656.event: The women take a ruby for kaya blossoms and hide their eyes from the bees.

1657.reading: The king's women, in the guise of watchers of a ripe hill-field, call to the parrots there in sweet lisping speech and coax them to come.
1657.nuance: Line 3 ends புனக்கிளிக and line 4 has மாயோன் மடந்தைமார்; the lost letter in line 3 is supplied as கிளிகளை, and 'the dark lord's women' is read as the king's women.
1657.event: The women call the parrots of the hill-field and delight them.

1658.reading: On the gem-set rocks of a gold hill covered with fresh leaves, some tender-bodied women gather in pleasant company.
1658.event: Some women gather on the rocks of the hill.

1659.reading: On the gold slab they set a coral for the pestle, pour in gems, lift the tusk, and, as the golden hill sounds, sing of the dark one in the rhythm of a pounding song.
1659.nuance: The pounding song (அம்மனை வள்ளை) turns grain-work into play with gems; the dark one of line 4 is the king, as the next verses' refrain shows.
1659.event: The women pound gems in play and sing of the dark lord.

1660.reading: The song names the dark cloud-hued one's deeds: he lifted a bow, tore open the lion's mouth, struck down the rutting elephant Ayakkiriva, and held the white hill.
1660.nuance: Verses 1660-1662 carry a refrain of the dark-hued one; the deeds named are of the song, and the verse does not tell them as events.
1660.event: The women sing the king's heroic deeds.

1661.reading: The song says he put the conch to his mouth and took the bow, saw the foe's head tremble in the war, and embraced the lotus-lady's gold body.
1661.nuance: The song joins war (conch, bow, enemy's trembling) and love (the lotus-lady's body) as the one fame of the king.
1661.event: The women sing the king's war and his embrace of the lotus-lady.

1662.reading: The song says he is the wearer of the golden discus and long crown, who took the wealth and ornaments of enemies and enjoyed the pleasures of the trusted lady.
1662.nuance: The same verse sets conquest and enjoyment side by side as his praise.
1662.event: The women sing of his wealth, his crown and his love.

1663.reading: While the women sing and the chief queen looks on, the king, his heart breaking at their joy in the others, calls a divine being near him and bids it become an elephant with a spread face-cloth.
1663.nuance: The whole verse joins a grieving heart and a ruse; the stated reason in line 2 and 3 is that love's flood and his breaking mind move him, and the poem calls the king's heart both hurt and playful. The text of the verse is printed in eight half-lines and repaired.
1663.event: The king, wishing to frighten the women, orders a god to take elephant form.

1664.reading: A god becomes an elephant like a dark mountain, with its rut flowing, and comes like a mountain nearing a millet field, so that the dark-eyed women tremble.
1664.event: The god in elephant form approaches the women, who tremble.

1665.reading: The women's dark hair slips about their sides, the rings in their ears swing, their spear-like eyes flicker, and they shake like peahens scattered by fear.
1665.event: The women tremble before the elephant.

1666.reading: A trembling woman looks about and cries for her lord's feet; he comes up, tells her not to fear, and says that he is here; he has done the great penance that brings whatever one wants.
1666.nuance: The last line gives the king's power as the fruit of a past penance; it states a claim about tapas in a verse of love-play, and speaks of the king as the hero of the ruse, not as one who has renounced.
1666.event: The king comes to the frightened woman and reassures her.

claims.claim: great penance brings whatever one desires

1667.reading: Turning the rutting elephant back, the king embraces the woman, sets a fragrant garland on her, tidies her clothes, smooths the ear-roll and sets her gold ornaments in place.
1667.event: The king drives off the elephant and comforts the woman.

1668.reading: After the dark-hued king has deceived all his women and comes down from the grove-hill, the sun stands at noon, burning the sky.
1668.event: The king comes down the hill at noon, having deceived the women.

1669.reading: Beads of sweat on the women's brows pull the king's heart, so he goes to the pool in the flowering grove to see them bathe.
1669.event: The king goes to the pool to watch the women bathe.

1670.reading: The attendants show the king pools of sandal-water, red lilies, golden lotuses and clear gem-blue water, and then bow and stand aside.
1670.nuance: Line 4 ends with a doubled காட்டி and the clause வாய்ந்தவை போல is hard to place; read as the attendants showing the pools.
1670.event: The attendants point out the pools to the king.

1671.reading: At the king's order that they hide, the attendants withdraw, and he enters the whirling pool with the women, whose gold-freckled breasts are pressed together.
1671.event: The king sends the attendants away and enters the pool with the women.

1672.reading: Water that comes down the gold channels from the gem stones fills the pool and swirls, and the women's floats lift on it.
1672.nuance: The verse describes the pool's source and its swirling; the connection of the waters with the women's floats in line 3 is read loosely.
1672.event: The pool fills and swirls as the women bathe.

1673.reading: As the water rises, some women cling to the sea-hued king like creepers to a hill, others seize a float and lose their garlands, and others lose their clothes and ear-ornaments and make for the shore.
1673.event: The rising water scatters the women, who cling to the king or flee.

1674.reading: With the swirling water drawing round him, the king stands firm in the pool, his eyes reddened, and the women begin a water-fight, flinging water on his chest.
1674.event: The king stands in the pool and the women start a water-fight against him.

links.note: 1663 has the king order a god to become an elephant; 1664 shows the god taking the shape and nearing the women.
links.teaches: The king's order is carried out at once, so the fear in the grove is the king's own design and not an accident.

links.note: 1666 has the king soothe the frightened woman; 1667 shows him driving off the elephant and adorning her.
links.teaches: The rescuer is the one who sent the danger, and the comfort completes his ruse.

links.note: 1635 has the women sing the king's fame; 1659 begins a pounding song whose next verses list his deeds.
links.teaches: The fame the women only named earlier is now given its content, war and love together, in the song.

links.note: 1669 sends the king to the pool to see the women bathe; 1674 has the bathing turn into a water-fight with him.
links.teaches: The watcher he meant to be becomes a target, so the pleasure goes from looking to joining.

links.note: 1666 ends by saying the king did a great penance that gives him whatever he wishes; Kural 265 gives wish-fulfilment as the reason penance is practised.
links.teaches: The wish that penance buys here is a prank to win an embrace, which tests whether the Kural's reason for tapas needs any worthy wish.

gains.a: 1666 gets a stated rule behind its claim, that penance pays in whatever is wanted, so the king's power reads as a fruit of tapas.
gains.b: Kural 265 gets a case where the wish bought is a trivial love-ruse, so its 'whatever is wished' is shown to cover small and worldly wishes.

links.note: 1663 names the rutting elephant with a spread face-cloth; Kural 1087 likens the cloth on a woman's breast to the face-cloth over a rutting elephant's eyes.
links.teaches: The same elephant's face-cloth marks erotic danger in a couplet and is used as a stage prop to scare women into a man's arms in the epic.

gains.a: 1663 gets the face-cloth read as the sign of a threat that is also desire, so the elephant's fright is a love-device.
gains.b: Kural 1087 gets a scene where such an elephant is actually set before women, showing the image as a danger they flee, not only as a metaphor.

source_issues: Verses 1663-1674 were printed in eight half-lines and repaired into four lines by the build; read as four. 1669 line 1 had a pulli removed after a vowel sign.
1657 line 3 ends புனக்கிளிக with a lost letter; 1670 line 4 has a doubled காட்டி and a doubtful போலக்காட்டி; those readings are marked uncertain.
